items.title: David Torkanowsky interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019
items.q: that’s kind of the way Smoky Johnson in New Orleans started playing funk.

ctx.x: Exactly. But you went through, the feel of the music changed as you progressed. And I think it has a lot to do with the series of eighth notes, whether they’re straight, whether they’re really swingy.

Well listen you know jazz was the popular music of a certain time. And then at some point rock & roll became the popular music. Now what was the transition? Well the eighth note was carrying the water. So in jazz music the eighth note we consider to be the first and last of a triplet [scats]. You know it’s interesting, when I teach young drummers how to swing on a cymbal I teach them, “Draw a quarter note on the left hand — draw a quarter note here, a dotted eighth here, and a sixteenth here. And put your stick…

It’s swinging. Secondly, you have to [scats] on the backbeat you have to lift the stick and travel so that puts it — that makes the cymbal pattern swing. So that illustrates the movable eighth note. Now I think what you’re asking me is, in swing [scats] you know the funky players, Phil Woods for example, he would straighten out eighth notes because that made him sound funky. Horace Silver, the two fathers of funk to me are Horace Silver and Professor Longhair. Professor Longhair comes more out of a Caribbean…
